hero.title: Nashik–Trimbakeshwar
hero.subtitle: Simhastha Kumbh Mela
hero.description: Once every twelve years, when Jupiter enters Leo, millions gather on the banks of the Godavari to take a sacred dip — a ritual unbroken since legend says drops of celestial nectar fell here.

sites.title: Two Sacred Sites
sites.description: Ramkund in Nashik city, and Kushavarta Kund at Trimbakeshwar, 30 km away — where the Godavari is born.

cycle.title: Once Every 12 Years
cycle.description: Timed to Jupiter's entry into Leo — this cycle runs an unusually long 21 months, ending July 2028.

pilgrims.title: Millions of Pilgrims
pilgrims.description: Over 30 million devotees attended in 2015 — 2027 is expected to draw even larger crowds.

ramkund.title: Ramkund, Nashik
ramkund.description: The river city of ritual memory. Tradition holds that Lord Rama bathed here during his exile — giving Ramkund its name and its place at the heart of the Vaishnavite Amrit Snan.

trimbakeshwar.title: Trimbakeshwar
trimbakeshwar.description: Home to one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva, and the source of the Godavari itself. The Shaivite akharas hold Trimbakeshwar as the original seat of the Mela.

history.label: Why it's celebrated
history.title: History & Mythology
history.paragraph1: The story begins long before Nashik existed as a city. According to the Puranas, the gods and demons once joined forces to churn the cosmic ocean in search of Amrit, the nectar of immortality. They used Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope, with Vishnu himself, in the form of a giant tortoise, steadying the mountain beneath the waves. As the ocean turned, it released both poison and treasure — Shiva drank the poison to save creation, and eventually the Kumbh, a pot brimming with Amrit, rose out of the water.
history.paragraph2: What followed was a chase, not a celebration. Gods and demons fought over the pot for twelve divine days — which, in human time, stretched to twelve years. As Garuda carried the Kumbh across the sky, four drops of nectar spilled to Earth, landing at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nashik. Each place absorbed a measure of that power, and each has held a Kumbh Mela ever since, roughly once every twelve years, timed to the same planetary rhythm that marked the original chase.
history.simhasthaAnswer: The Mela is named for the moment it occurs, not the place. It falls when Jupiter — Guru, the teacher of the gods — moves into Leo (Simha) in Vedic astrology, an alignment that recurs roughly once every twelve years. Nashik and Ujjain share this particular alignment, which is why their Kumbh Melas both carry the name Simhastha, distinct from the Haridwar and Prayagraj gatherings.
history.paragraph4: Nashik's claim to the tradition runs deeper than astrology alone. The region is part of the Dandakaranya forest where the Ramayana places Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana during their years of exile — which is why the bathing spot in Nashik city is named Ramkund, "Rama's pool." Thirty kilometres away, Trimbakeshwar holds one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva and marks the source of the Godavari river itself — giving the Simhastha its dual character, shared between a Vaishnavite city and a Shaivite source.
history.paragraph5: Today, the ritual stays remarkably close to what it has always been. Pilgrims bathe in the Godavari believing it dissolves the weight of past karma; akharas process through the streets ahead of each Amrit Snan; and for a few months, caste, region, and background fall away in a crowd united by nothing but the river and the calendar.
history.twelveYearsQuestion: Why does it happen every twelve years?
history.twelveYearsAnswer: The answer lies in both mythology and astronomy. According to tradition, the struggle between the gods and demons for the Kumbh of Amrit lasted twelve divine days, which came to symbolize twelve human years. In astronomical terms, Jupiter — known as Guru or Brihaspati in Vedic astrology — takes nearly twelve years to complete one journey through the zodiac. Simhastha is celebrated when Jupiter returns to Leo (Simha Rashi) and aligns with specific positions of the Sun and Moon, recreating the celestial conditions associated with the original legend. This rare alignment is why Nashik's Simhastha Kumbh Mela is held only once every twelve years.

flag.title: Dhwajarohan (Flag Hoisting)
flag.desc: The Simhastha Kumbh Mela begins with a ceremonial flag hoisting at Ramkund, Nashik and Trimbakeshwar.

parikrama.title: Nagar Parikrama
parikrama.desc: Devotees and saints perform a sacred procession around Nashik city. (Date subject to final confirmation by the Akhada Parishad.)

firstSnan.title: First Amrit Snan
firstSnan.desc: First holy dip in the Godavari river during Shravan Shuddha, marking the formal opening of the bathing phase.

secondSnan.title: Second Amrit Snan
secondSnan.desc: Shravan Amavasya holy dip — regarded as the most spiritually potent bathing day, attended by millions of devotees.

thirdSnan.title: Third Amrit Snan
thirdSnan.desc: Bhadrapada Shukla Ekadashi holy dip at Ramkund, Nashik, concluding the royal bathing cycle.

conclusion.title: Conclusion Ceremony
conclusion.desc: Official conclusion of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela, after a sacred cycle of nearly 21 months.

amritSnan.title: Amrit Snan
amritSnan.description: The royal bath, led by the akharas in order of precedence — the most sacred and most crowded ritual of the Mela.

akhada.title: Akhada Procession
akhada.description: Sacred marches of sadhus, elephants, and chariots toward the river ahead of each Amrit Snan.

holyDip.title: Holy Dip
holyDip.description: Open to every pilgrim throughout the Parva days — bathing in the Godavari is believed to cleanse karmic sin.

simhastha.a: The name comes from "Simha," the Leo zodiac sign. The Mela is held when Jupiter enters Leo — an alignment that occurs roughly once every 12 years.

pass.q: Do I need a pass to attend?
pass.a: No. Entry to the Kumbh Mela is free for all pilgrims. Special arrangements are made for the Amrit Snan days due to the scale of the crowds.

dates.q: Are the Amrit Snan dates final?
dates.a: The dates listed follow current astrological calculations and government notifications. Final muhurtas are confirmed closer to the event by the Akhada Parishad.

travel.q: How do I get to Nashik?
travel.a: Nashik is well connected by rail and road from Mumbai (~180 km) and Pune (~210 km). During the Mela, the state runs additional trains, buses, and shuttle services to Trimbakeshwar.

travel.title: Planning Your Visit
travel.description: Nashik is well connected by road and rail from Mumbai and Pune. During the Mela, special trains, buses, and shuttle services run to Trimbakeshwar, alongside expanded medical and accommodation facilities for the millions of expected visitors.

hero.label: A Stratigraphy of Nashik · 2000 BCE — Today
hero.title: History & Culture
hero.description: Four thousand years don't stack neatly. They settle in layers — myth pressed under empire, empire under devotion, devotion under steel and vineyard. Scroll down through the strata.

vedic.title: Nashik in Ancient Texts
vedic.description: Nashik, known in ancient times as Padmavati, Janasthana, and Trinkha, holds a sacred place in Indian mythology and early history. It is prominently mentioned in the Ramayana, where Lord Rama, along with Sita and Lakshmana, spent a significant part of their 14-year exile in the forest region of Panchavati. Sages performed rituals, meditation, and teaching along its riverbanks, shaping its identity as a pilgrimage destination for centuries to come.

buddhist.title: A Center of Monks and Merchants
buddhist.description: Under the Satavahana dynasty, Nashik emerged as a major center for Buddhism and trade. Its most remarkable legacy is the Pandav Leni caves — 24 rock-cut monasteries and prayer halls carved into the Trirashmi hills. Inscriptions found there record donors, merchants, and rulers, evidence of a city thriving on trade routes connecting northern and southern India.

satavahana.title: Provincial Capital
satavahana.description: By 100 CE, Nashik had become an administrative and economic center under the Satavahanas. Inscriptions in the Nashik caves from this period are among the most important historical records of the dynasty, naming kings, traders, and monks. Economic stability and religious tolerance laid the foundation for the city's long-term importance.

medieval.title: Rise of Shaiva Worship
medieval.description: Nashik grew into a major center for Shaivism, the worship of Lord Shiva. The Trimbakeshwar Temple, one of the twelve sacred Jyotirlingas, was established in this period and became a major pilgrimage site. The Godavari's origin nearby deepened the city's religious standing — pilgrims arrived in growing numbers to bathe and seek blessings.

yadava.title: Temples in Black Stone
yadava.description: Under the Yadavas, ruling from Devagiri, Nashik saw significant growth in temple architecture, much of it in the Hemadpanthi style — dense, dark basalt carved with intricate detail. Proximity to the Godavari kept Nashik a pilgrimage destination, while trade and agriculture expanded alongside it.

maratha.title: Kalaram Temple Built
maratha.description: Sardar Rangarao Odhekar built the Kalaram Temple in Panchavati after the Maratha victory era, dedicating it to a black-stone idol of Rama recovered from the Godavari. The Trimbakeshwar Temple was also rebuilt and expanded under Peshwa Balaji Bajirao, cementing Nashik's place as both a spiritual and administrative center.

british.title: Colonial Administration Begins
british.description: After the Marathas' defeat in the Third Anglo-Maratha War, Nashik came under British rule. The East India Company built roads, government offices, and a central jail, introducing Western education and legal systems — modernizing infrastructure while unsettling traditional local autonomy.

satyagraha.title: Kalaram Temple Entry Satyagraha
satyagraha.description: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar led a landmark protest at the Kalaram Temple, demanding the right for Dalits to enter Hindu temples. Thousands joined the peaceful demonstration. Though immediate temple entry was not won, the satyagraha became a defining moment in India's struggle against caste-based exclusion.

independence.title: An Industrial City Takes Shape
independence.description: After independence, Nashik transformed into a major industrial hub. MIDC zones drew engineering, manufacturing, and defense industries — including the Currency Note Press and an Ordnance Factory — balancing the city's ancient religious identity with new economic weight.

modern.title: India's Wine Capital
modern.description: Favorable climate and soil turned Nashik into India's wine country, anchored by Sula Vineyards and now home to over 100 wineries. Annual festivals and wine tourism draw visitors nationwide — a modern layer atop four millennia of sacred and political history.

intro.label: One layer, many identities
intro.title: What Makes Nashik Different
intro.description: Most Indian cities pick one identity and keep it. Nashik never picked just one — it's a pilgrimage town, a grape-growing district, and a wine region, all running at the same time, all genuinely true.

grapeCapital.title: India's Grape Capital
grapeCapital.description: Nashik is the country's leading grape producer, growing more than half of India's grape exports. The same hills that grow table grapes also feed its wine industry.

wineCapital.title: India's Wine Capital
wineCapital.description: Home to over 50 wineries, including Sula — the winery that put Indian wine on the map in 1999. Roughly half of all wineries in Maharashtra sit in this one district.

pilgrimageCity.title: A Living Pilgrimage City
pilgrimageCity.description: Trimbakeshwar's Jyotirlinga, Ramkund, and Panchavati aren't museum pieces — they're active sites of daily worship, exactly as they've been for centuries.

onionCapital.title: The Onion Capital, Too
onionCapital.description: Less photographed than the vineyards, but just as real: Nashik district is one of India's largest onion-producing regions, especially around Lasalgaon's wholesale market.

kumbhSite.title: One of Four Kumbh Sites
kumbhSite.description: Nashik-Trimbakeshwar is one of only four places in India that host the Kumbh Mela, alongside Haridwar, Prayagraj, and Ujjain — sharing the Simhastha cycle with Ujjain alone.

westernGhats.title: Western Ghats on Its Doorstep
westernGhats.description: Hill forts, the Anjneri range, and trekking country sit within an hour of the city center — a side of Nashik that rarely makes the postcards.

varanasi.label: vs. Varanasi
varanasi.description: Both are sacred river cities, but Nashik pairs its temples with a modern wine industry — a combination no other Indian pilgrimage city offers.

goa.label: vs. Goa
goa.description: Where Goa built its identity around beaches, Nashik built one around vineyards in the hills — India's closest answer to wine country, without the coastline.

pune.label: vs. Pune
pune.description: Pune is the bigger metro nearby, but Nashik holds the older, deeper religious history — the Ramayana connection runs through Nashik, not Pune.

hero.title: About Explore Nashik
hero.description: A digital guide to Nashik's temples, vineyards, food, and hidden corners — built by two people who wanted one place that actually covers all of it.

whyExists.label: Why this exists
whyExists.paragraph1: We kept noticing the same thing: information about Nashik was scattered across ten different blogs, none of them current, half of them written for a city that's changed since. The temple hours were wrong, the "hidden gem" cafés had closed down, and nobody mentioned that the wine tour and the Kumbh Mela calendar might matter to the same traveler.
whyExists.paragraph2: So we're building the version we wanted to find — one place for heritage, food, travel logistics, and the practical stuff like distances and emergency numbers. No ads deciding what you see first, no listicle padding. Just what's actually useful, kept up to date by two people who live here.

wineTourism.title: Nashik Wine Country
wineTourism.description: Nashik produces over 40% of India's wine. With 100+ wineries in the region, experience world-class wine tourism amid the beautiful Sahyadri hills. From Sula to York, embark on an unforgettable vineyard trail.

seo.title: Travel Information | Explore Nashik
seo.description: Travel information, transport guide and useful tips for visiting Nashik.

hero.label: Routes In · Routes Around
hero.title: Travel Information
hero.description: By road, rail, or air — how to get to Nashik, how to move once you're here, and what to know before you go.

winter.highlights: Perfect for sightseeing, wine tours, and outdoor activities

summer.highlights: Plan indoor attractions; early morning temple visits

monsoon.highlights: Dugarwadi Waterfall at best; Gangapur Dam scenic; avoid trekking

byAir.title: By Air
byAir.description: Ozar Airport (IATA: ISK) is 24 km from Nashik city. It has limited commercial flights. The nearest major airport is Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, Mumbai (165 km).
byAir.tips: Most travelers fly into Mumbai and take a road or rail connection to Nashik.

byRail.title: By Train
byRail.description: Nashik Road Railway Station is the main railway station, well-connected to major Indian cities. Mumbai Central to Nashik takes 3-4 hours. Many Rajdhani and Express trains stop here.
byRail.tips: Nashik Road station is 8 km from city center. Autos and taxis available.

byRoad.title: By Road
byRoad.description: Nashik is very well-connected by road. NH-3 (Mumbai-Agra Highway) passes through Nashik. Excellent bus services from Mumbai, Pune, and other Maharashtra cities.
byRoad.tips: Shivneri (MSRTC AC Volvo) buses from Mumbai are comfortable and frequent. Book online at msrtcotix.in

autoRickshaw.description: Metered autos available throughout the city. Insist on meter or agree price before boarding.
autoRickshaw.tips: Readily available, fastest for short distances

cityBus.description: MSRTC city buses connect major areas. Routes cover Panchvati, MIDC, Satpur, Gangapur.
cityBus.tips: Cheapest option, but can be crowded and slow

appCab.description: Ola and Uber available in Nashik. Good for comfortable point-to-point travel.
appCab.tips: Best for airport transfers and late-night travel

rentedBike.description: Available from rental shops near railway station. Great for vineyard hopping and exploring at your own pace.
rentedBike.tips: International driving license required for some rentals

cycleRickshaw.description: Available in the old city and near Panchvati area. Eco-friendly for short distances.
cycleRickshaw.tips: Good for exploring the Panchvati area

taxiDayHire.description: Full-day taxi hire for visiting multiple attractions. Best for Trimbakeshwar, Saptashringi trips.
taxiDayHire.tips: Negotiate rates beforehand; AC vehicles recommended in summer

travelTips.title: Travel Tips
travelTips.subtitle: Essential information to plan your perfect Nashik trip

bestTime.title: Best Time
bestTime.desc: October to March for pleasant weather. Monsoon (July-Sept) for waterfalls and lush greenery.

howToReach.title: How to Reach
howToReach.desc: Via Mumbai (3hrs road/rail), Pune (4hrs), or fly to Mumbai and drive.

language.title: Language
language.desc: Marathi is the local language. Hindi and English widely understood.

topAttraction.title: Must-Try Food in Nashik
topAttraction.subtitle: Discover the best restaurants, cafes, and local flavors in Nashik

misalPav.name: Misal Pav
misalPav.description: Nashik's iconic spicy Misal served with pav, farsan, onions, and lemon.

sabudanaVada.name: Sabudana Vada
sabudanaVada.description: Crispy sabudana fritters served with coconut and peanut chutney.

kandaBhaji.name: Kanda Bhaji
kandaBhaji.description: Crispy onion fritters best enjoyed during monsoon evenings.

pavwada.name: Pavwada
pavwada.description: Authentic Maharashtrian Pavwada, a popular street food served with spicy chutney and traditional flavors.

kalaMuttonRassa.name: Kala Mutton Rassa
kalaMuttonRassa.description: Traditional Maharashtrian black mutton curry prepared with roasted spices, coconut, and a rich, spicy gravy. Its bold flavor and authentic taste stand out.

puranPoli.name: Puran Poli
puranPoli.description: Puran Poli is a traditional Maharashtrian sweet flatbread stuffed with a delicious mixture of jaggery and chana dal. It is especially popular during festivals and celebrations for its rich taste and cultural significance.

topAttractions.title: Top Attractions
topAttractions.subtitle: Essential information to plan your perfect Nashik trip

trimbakeshwarTemple.name: Trimbakeshwar Temple
trimbakeshwarTemple.description: One of the twelve sacred Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva and a major pilgrimage destination in India.

sulaVineyards.name: Sula Vineyards
sulaVineyards.description: India's most famous winery offering vineyard tours, wine tastings, and stunning views of the surrounding hills.

hariharFort.name: Harihar Fort
hariharFort.description: Famous for its steep rock-cut staircase and breathtaking trekking experience.

ramkund.name: Ramkund
ramkund.description: Sacred bathing ghat on the Godavari River, an important pilgrimage site.

kalaramTemple.name: Kalaram Temple
kalaramTemple.description: Historic temple dedicated to Lord Rama, known for its black stone architecture.

saptashrungiDeviTemple.name: Saptashrungi Devi Temple
saptashrungiDeviTemple.description: One of Maharashtra's most revered Shakti Peethas, located amidst seven hills.
